description: How the Volstead Act tried to dry out America — and what bootleggers and speakeasies did with it.
content_html:
America Goes Dry

On 17 January 1920, the Prohibition came into force across the United States. The 18th Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in January 1919, had banned the production, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors. The Volstead Act, passed in October 1919, defined the legal threshold (anything over 0.5 per cent alcohol) and gave enforcement powers to federal agents. The ambition was sweeping: to eliminate drunkenness, domestic violence, poverty, and crime by removing alcohol from American life. The reality was very different.

Key Fact

Prohibition grew from three overlapping movements: the Protestant temperance movement, which had campaigned for decades against drinking as a moral evil; the Progressive reformers, who argued that alcohol was the root cause of urban poverty and domestic abuse; and a strand of nativism, which associated alcohol with German beer halls and southern European wine-drinking immigrants. The Anti-Saloon League, led by Wayne Wheeler, co-ordinated this coalition and was the most effective single-issue pressure group in American history to that point.

Enforcement and Its Failures

From the outset, Prohibition was extraordinarily difficult to enforce. The Volstead Act created a federal Prohibition Bureau, but it was chronically underfunded and its agents were notoriously susceptible to bribery. In 1920, there were only about 1,500 agents covering the entire country. Large sections of the American public — particularly in cities, among immigrant communities, and in wealthier social circles — had no intention of stopping drinking.

Illegal drinking establishments, known as speakeasies, multiplied across American cities. New York City, which had roughly 15,000 legal bars before Prohibition, was estimated to have between 20,000 and 30,000 speakeasies by the late 1920s. Bootleggers supplied them through a combination of domestic illegal distillation, smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean, and the diversion of industrial alcohol.

Key Fact

Al Capone’s organisation in Chicago demonstrated how far Prohibition had failed. By the late 1920s, Capone’s criminal network was earning an estimated $60 million a year from bootlegging, gambling, and other illegal activities. He employed hundreds of people and had bribed significant numbers of police officers and city officials. The St Valentine’s Day Massacre of February 1929, in which seven members of a rival gang were shot dead, showed the murderous competition for control of bootlegging territory. Capone was eventually convicted — not for bootlegging but for tax evasion — in 1931.

Prohibition accelerated the growth of organised crime in American cities. Criminal networks that had previously focused on gambling and prostitution expanded massively into the alcohol trade, using violence to enforce territory and corruption to neutralise law enforcement. Federal agent Eliot Ness and his team, nicknamed the “Untouchables” for their refusal to take bribes, became famous for their raids on Capone’s breweries — but their victories were largely tactical rather than strategic. The Capone organisation survived and adapted repeatedly.

Corruption was not limited to Chicago. In major cities across the country, Prohibition created a system in which police, judges, and politicians accepted payment to allow the illegal trade to operate. This widespread corruption damaged public respect for law enforcement and the legal system more broadly, contributing to the eventual political momentum for repeal.

The Road to Repeal

Support for Prohibition weakened through the late 1920s and collapsed during the Great Depression. The economic argument shifted decisively: a legal alcohol industry would generate tax revenue and jobs at precisely the moment the government needed both. The Association Against the Prohibition Amendment, funded by wealthy industrialists, lobbied effectively for repeal. Franklin Roosevelt, who supported repeal, won the 1932 election in a landslide. The 21st Amendment, ratified in December 1933, ended Prohibition — the only time a constitutional amendment has been repealed in American history.

Historians note that Prohibition was not a total failure. Alcohol consumption did fall significantly in the early years of Prohibition — cirrhosis death rates dropped, arrests for public drunkenness declined, and there is evidence of reduced domestic violence in some areas. But these gains were largely reversed as the bootlegging economy grew. By the mid-1920s, drinking was widespread again, concentrated in cities and among the middle class. The rural Protestant communities that had driven Prohibition remained broadly supportive throughout, while urban, immigrant, and working-class communities rejected it consistently.
exam_tip_html: Questions on Prohibition often ask you to explain its failure. Make sure you address multiple causes rather than focusing only on Al Capone. Strong answers will discuss: the inadequacy of enforcement (too few agents, widespread bribery); the lack of public support in cities and among immigrant communities; the growth of organised crime; and the economic arguments that strengthened during the Depression. The repeal in 1933 is itself evidence of failure — use the 21st Amendment as a specific piece of evidence for your conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prohibition (1920–1933) was driven by the temperance movement, Progressive reformers, and nativist sentiment, co-ordinated by the Anti-Saloon League under Wayne Wheeler.
  • Enforcement was chronically underfunded and corrupt; speakeasies multiplied and Al Capone’s criminal network earned an estimated $60 million a year from bootlegging, demonstrating the scale of non-compliance.
  • The 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition in December 1933 — the only constitutional amendment ever to repeal a previous one — as economic arguments for tax revenue and jobs combined with widespread public rejection of the law.

practice_questions.text: Outline two causes of Prohibition in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each cause scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example causes: the temperance movement (1), which had campaigned for decades on religious and moral grounds against the harm caused by alcohol consumption (1); nativist hostility to immigrant drinking cultures (1), particularly aimed at German, Italian, and Irish communities who ran saloons (1); Progressive reform arguments (1) that alcohol was the root cause of urban poverty, domestic abuse, and crime (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Prohibition failed to eliminate alcohol consumption in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the Prohibition Bureau was underfunded with roughly 1,500 agents for the entire country, making enforcement impossible, and agents were susceptible to bribery from criminal networks like Capone’s; speakeasies multiplied to an estimated 20,000–30,000 in New York alone, supplied by bootleggers smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both reasons identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why organised crime grew so rapidly during the Prohibition era.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies and explains how Prohibition created a market for illegal alcohol that criminal networks could exploit; the enormous profits generated (Capone’s estimated $60 million annual income) funded expansion into other criminal activities; corruption of police and officials removed legal obstacles; violence enforced territory. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about crime increasing without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the St Valentine's Day Massacre of 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The massacre occurred in February 1929 in Chicago (1); seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were shot dead by gunmen believed to be linked to Al Capone’s organisation (1). Feature 2: The massacre illustrated the violent competition for control of bootlegging territory between rival criminal gangs (1); it shocked public opinion and increased pressure for both law enforcement action and a reconsideration of Prohibition (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Prohibition was a complete failure? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges partial successes (reduced alcohol consumption in early years, lower cirrhosis rates, fewer arrests for public drunkenness) before explaining why overall failure is the stronger conclusion (widespread non-compliance, growth of organised crime, corruption of officials, eventual repeal in 1933); uses specific evidence throughout and engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument addressing both success and failure with relevant evidence. Developing: Some awareness of both sides with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of Prohibition. Interpretation A argues it was a misguided moral experiment that gave power to criminals. Interpretation B argues it achieved real health and social benefits that were undermined by poor enforcement. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (moral vs. pragmatic framing, role of enforcement, health data); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (crime statistics for A; cirrhosis and domestic violence data for B); explains why interpretations differ (different evidence base, writing from different periods, urban vs. rural perspective). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the name of the Act that defined alcohol over 0.5% and gave enforcement powers during Prohibition?
Al Capone was eventually convicted in 1931 for which crime?
Prohibition was ended by the _____ Amendment, ratified in December 1933.
The most powerful lobbying organisation behind Prohibition was the _____, led by Wayne Wheeler.
Match each term to its correct definition during Prohibition.
right: Constitutional ban on alcohol production and sale

glossary_terms.definition: The nationwide ban on the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcohol, enforced in the USA from January 1920 to December 1933 under the 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act.
A movement opposing the consumption of alcohol, rooted in Protestant religious beliefs that alcohol was morally destructive and socially harmful.
The belief that American culture should be dominated by white Anglo-Saxon Protestant values, often directed against immigrants and their drinking customs.
The most powerful lobbying organisation behind Prohibition, led by Wayne Wheeler, which pressed politicians to vote for the 18th Amendment.
Illegal bars operating during Prohibition, often hidden behind innocent-looking storefronts, where customers could buy alcohol and socialise away from police attention.
People who illegally manufactured or distributed alcohol during Prohibition, often in organised criminal networks.
